ai.title: Brachial Plexus Injury
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The brachial plexus is a network of nerves from C5–T1 that supplies the upper limb. Injury patterns depend on the level and mechanism, with common causes in low‑resource settings including birth trauma, falls, and penetrating injuries.

b: Branches: musculocutaneous, axillary, median, ulnar, radial
sections.p: The brachial plexus forms from the ventral rami of C5–T1, arching over the first rib and dividing into roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and branches that innervate the shoulder, arm and hand.

b: Roots lie in the posterior triangle of the neck
Cords are named by their relation to the axillary artery
sections.p: Roots emerge from the intervertebral foramina, join to form trunks behind the clavicle, split into divisions, then cords around the axillary artery.

b: Roots are close to the brachial plexus
Trunks lie over the first rib
Cords run beside the axillary artery
sections.p: The plexus lies anterior to the scalene muscles, posterior to the clavicle, and is surrounded by the subclavius and suprascapular muscles.

b: Costocervical trunk supplies deep cervical vessels
Axillary artery gives posterior circumflex humeral artery
sections.p: The plexus receives arterial supply from the thyrocervical trunk, costocervical trunk, and axillary artery.
Motor branches innervate deltoid, biceps, triceps, forearm flexors and extensors; sensory branches supply the lateral arm, forearm and hand.

b: C8–T1: hand grip and fine movements
sections.p: Provides movement and sensation to the upper limb, enabling flexion, abduction, rotation and fine motor control.

b: Traumatic rupture: complete loss of function
sections.p: Injury mechanisms vary from birth trauma to penetrating wounds. Severity is graded by the Seddon or Sunderland systems, with complete tears requiring surgery.
